query: For structural materials intended for fusion plasma-facing components, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis explains what governs high-temperature plastic strain and toughness, and why? Specify a controlled comparison that would isolate the hypothesized cause, the observations predicted relative to an unperturbed baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, the prior evidence supporting it, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In structural materials for fusion plasma-facing components, high-temperature plastic strain and toughness are primarily governed by the stability and mobility of grain boundaries, specifically the propensity for grain boundary sliding and migration under thermal and irradiation conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: Polycrystalline metallic alloy (e.g., reduced-activation ferritic/martensitic steel or tungsten) with well-characterized grain size and boundary character distribution.
generation.intervention: Modify the grain boundary character distribution by thermomechanical processing to increase the fraction of low-angle or special (e.g., Σ3) boundaries versus random high-angle boundaries, while keeping grain size and composition constant.
generation.conditions: High-temperature mechanical testing (e.g., 0.5–0.8 Tm) under uniaxial tension or bending, with and without concurrent irradiation (e.g., He or neutron surrogate).
generation.structural_mediator: Grain boundary structure and mobility (fraction of special vs. random boundaries, grain boundary sliding activity).
generation.mechanism: At high temperatures, grain boundary sliding and migration accommodate plastic strain. Boundaries with higher mobility (random high-angle) facilitate plasticity but may also act as sites for void nucleation and crack propagation, reducing toughness. Increasing the fraction of low-mobility boundaries suppresses sliding, reducing plastic strain and potentially increasing toughness.
generation.predicted_outcome: Materials with a higher fraction of low-angle or special grain boundaries will exhibit reduced high-temperature plastic strain and increased toughness compared to baseline materials with predominantly random high-angle boundaries, under otherwise identical conditions.
generation.baseline: Material with as-received or conventionally processed grain boundary character distribution (predominantly random high-angle boundaries).
generation.boundary: Hypothesis holds for polycrystalline metallic alloys with grain sizes in the micron range, tested at temperatures above 0.5 Tm, and in the absence of severe grain growth or amorphization.
generation.uncertainty: Direct evidence for the dominant role of grain boundary character in fusion-relevant alloys under irradiation is limited; other mechanisms (e.g., dislocation climb, precipitation) may also contribute.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples with identical composition and grain size but differing grain boundary character distributions (one enriched in special boundaries, one with random boundaries). Subject both to high-temperature tensile tests with and without irradiation. Measure plastic strain to failure and fracture toughness.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If samples with increased special boundary fraction do not show reduced plastic strain and increased toughness relative to baseline, or if grain boundary character has no measurable effect, the hypothesis is falsified.
